query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a specific element to form a coherent nanoprecipitate phase within the eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility by facilitating dislocation transmission and relieving stress concentrations.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar structure
generation.intervention: Addition of a specific element (e.g., Cr) to form a coherent nanoprecipitate phase
generation.mechanism: Dislocation transmission and stress concentration relief
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength and room-temperature tensile ductility
generation.baseline: Unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar structure
generation.boundary: Limited to eutectic high-entropy alloys with a specific composition and microstructure
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and processing conditions required to achieve the desired nanoprecipitate phase and improved properties are uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing of the modified eutectic high-entropy alloy with and without the added element
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of the element does not result in improved strength and ductility, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Mechanism with scope. Mechanism: Coherent interfaces of nanoprecipitates facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations, preventing premature crack initiation and maintaining ductility while providing strength.. System: (W 1.5 Ni 2.25 Fe) 95 Ta 5 (at.%) refractory high-entropy alloy with stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). Conditions: Ambient temperature and 800 °C; tensile deformation up to 14% strain; after stepwise thermo-mechanical processing (cold rolling, annealing at 900 °C, aging at 650 °C). Evidence: measured. Observation: Dislocations cut through δ-lamellae and are pinned by γ″ particles; shearing of δ-lamellae leads to coherent misalignment rather than microcrack formation at 14% strain.. Scope limits: Does not hold for traditional alloys with brittle secondary phases (e.g., silicides, B2, Laves) or intermetallic compounds at grain boundaries which cause embrittlement.. Alternatives: Single precipitation processes (limited strengthening potency) and non-coherent precipitates (cause brittle fracture).. Mechanism: The pseudo-binary nature of the alloy (NiAl-rich B2 phase and Co/Cr/Fe-rich fcc phase) allows for the design of a composite structure that balances the low ductility of NiAl with the high strength of the fcc phase.. System: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA (regarded as a highly concentrated pseudo-binary NiAl/(Co, Cr, Fe) eutectic alloy). Conditions: As-cast state; room temperature and high temperature (up to 700°C). Evidence: inferred. Observation: The alloy exhibited a much higher fracture strength and simultaneously much higher ductility at room temperature compared to NiAl or NiAl/Cr(Mo) eutectic alloys.. Scope limits: Relies on the specific phase constitution of fcc and B2; the authors state the mechanism for the low elastic limit is unclear.. Alternatives: NiAl alloys which have low ductility at room temperature and low strength at high temperatures.. Quote: "The current EHEA can be regarded as a highly concentrated pseudo-binary NiAl/(Co, Cr, Fe) eutectic alloy."
